metadata.narrative: Conduct a comprehensive historical analysis of how the world has changed since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Compare and contrast life before COVID and after it, covering key domains such as public health, work culture, education, travel, economy, mental health, social interactions, and technology adoption. Provide deep, well-researched insights and include real-world examples to support your points. Structure the analysis in chronological order (from the pre-pandemic era, through the initial outbreak in early 2020, the global response, vaccine rollouts, to the 2025 post-pandemic lifestyle) to enhance clarity and understanding. Aim for thoroughness and detail to ensure all major global shifts and trends are captured.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Before COVID-19 upended daily life, only about 23 percent of US employees ever worked from home, and Pew Research found the figure closer to 7 percent for those doing so full time, meaning remote work was mostly a perk for highly paid white-collar professionals.
Global travel, in-person schooling, and face-to-face socializing were the unquestioned default, and video-conferencing tools existed but were used by a small niche rather than entire populations.
The origin story begins in Wuhan, China, where the first coronavirus cluster was reported on December 31, 2019, and China became the first country to close schools nationwide on January 26, 2020.
By February 2020 the virus had been named COVID-19 and cases had appeared in Thailand and the United States, and the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a global pandemic on March 11, 2020.

Within days the United States declared a national emergency, and financial markets convulsed, with the Dow Jones posting three separate crashes in March 2020 known as "Black Monday I," "Black Thursday," and "Black Monday II."

Governments worldwide responded with sweeping lockdowns, and the International Monetary Fund projected the global economy would shrink over 3 percent in 2020, the steepest slowdown since the Great Depression.

The World Bank later confirmed global GDP fell 5.2 percent in 2020, marking the first contraction of emerging-market economies since 1960 and pushing an estimated 70 to 100 million people into extreme poverty.

In the United States alone more than 36 million people filed for unemployment benefits within weeks, while European economies like France, Spain, and Italy saw GDP plunge by 17 to 21 percent in a single quarter.
Governments answered with historic stimulus, including the United States' $2 trillion CARES Act, worth roughly 10 percent of GDP, alongside comparable packages in Japan and Germany.

Education was upended just as dramatically, with 1.7 billion students forced out of school worldwide, and studies in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Pakistan documented severe rural-urban learning gaps as remote instruction reached wealthier households far more effectively than poorer ones.

A Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel report estimated a potential $17 trillion loss in lifetime earnings for affected schoolchildren, citing data showing Sao Paulo students in remote classes learned nearly 75 percent less than peers in person.

Air travel collapsed almost overnight, with global passenger traffic falling nearly 66 percent in 2020 according to IATA, industry net losses exceeding $118 billion, and carriers including Flybe, Virgin Australia, LATAM, and Avianca ceasing operations or filing for bankruptcy.

Isolation and uncertainty triggered a new mental health crisis, with depression rates nearly tripling to almost 30 percent in the pandemic's early months and drug overdose deaths topping 100,000 between April 2020 and April 2021.

Forced physical distancing reshaped social bonds, as academic analysis found people lost "weak ties" and gathered into smaller, more homogeneous networks, while everyday gestures like handshakes and hugs, documented in Romania, were replaced by elbow bumps and distanced greetings.

Amid the devastation, technology adoption accelerated at unprecedented speed, as remote work jumped almost overnight to roughly a third of employed Americans, video-conferencing app downloads hit a record 62 million in a single week, and e-commerce, telemedicine, and e-learning platforms all saw surging demand.

Hope arrived at the close of 2020 when Moderna and Pfizer/BioNTech announced highly effective vaccine candidates, with the FDA granting emergency authorization to Pfizer on December 11, 2020, Moderna a week later, and Johnson & Johnson in February 2021.

Throughout 2021 vaccine mandates spread across employers, healthcare systems, and the military, the United States hit President Biden's goal of 70 percent adult vaccination by early August, and boosters were rolled out as the Delta and later Omicron variants eroded vaccine efficacy against infection.

A brief pause in Johnson & Johnson distribution in April 2021, prompted by rare blood-clot reports, was lifted within ten days after safety review, illustrating both caution and resilience in the rollout.

As economies reopened, a global supply chain crisis and inflation surge followed, with commodity prices rising 31 to 60 percent above pre-pandemic levels, natural gas prices climbing over 500 percent, and a semiconductor shortage disrupting more than 169 industries.

The labor market underwent its own upheaval as the "Great Resignation" saw more than 47 million Americans quit their jobs in 2021 alone, followed by "quiet quitting," a trend Gallup's 2022 workplace report linked to just 21 percent of employees feeling engaged.
The United States formally ended its COVID-19 public health emergency declaration on May 11, 2023, marking the transition from pandemic crisis toward an endemic, manageable disease.

By the mid-2020s, remote work had settled well below its pandemic peak but far above pre-2020 norms, with fully remote US workers falling to about 12 percent by 2023 even as a quarter of the workforce retained hybrid arrangements, and Upwork projecting 32.6 million Americans would still work remotely by 2025.

This settling did not come without friction, as corporate leaders like Amazon's Andy Jassy pushed for full in-office returns, arguing employees perform better on-site despite acknowledging a lack of supporting data.

Education technology investment illustrated the scale of lasting change, projected to grow from $18 billion in 2019 to roughly $350 billion by 2025, even as most students returned to physical classrooms.

Long COVID emerged as a lasting medical legacy, with a large Scottish study finding persistent symptoms in 13.8 percent of infected people at six months, rising to 16.3 percent at eighteen months, while global estimates by 2024 placed long-COVID sufferers above 65 million worldwide.
Even years later, COVID-19 continued to carry a higher mortality risk than seasonal influenza, underscoring that its transition to endemic status did not mean the disease had become harmless.

Taken together, the arc from a near-total absence of remote work and digital healthcare in 2019 to a world where hybrid work, telehealth, e-learning, and lingering long-COVID burdens are permanent fixtures illustrates how thoroughly the pandemic reorganized public health, workplaces, schools, travel, economies, and social life within a single half-decade.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

Conduct a comprehensive historical analysis of how the world has changed since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Compare and contrast life before COVID and after it, covering key domains such as public health, work culture, education, travel, economy, mental health, social interactions, and technology adoption. Provide deep, well-researched insights and include real-world examples to support your points. Structure the analysis in chronological order (from the pre-pandemic era, through the initial outbreak in early 2020, the global response, vaccine rollouts, to the 2025 post-pandemic lifestyle) to enhance clarity and understanding. tools.name: search
tools.description: Search the available evidence corpus. Results contain ranked document IDs and document text; inspect that text directly and cite by docid. Each result is bounded independently before it is staged.

query.description: A natural-language query for evidence relevant to the research request.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

budget_tokens_per_result.description: Maximum approximate tokens staged per result. Text is bounded at tokens × 5 characters and cut at the final line break before that boundary. Default 4096.

tools.name: commit_context
tools.description: Select the small subset of documents from the MOST RECENT staged search batch whose full text should persist. This MUST be the first control action on the immediately following model turn. Every staged occurrence not listed is compacted before the next turn. Do not select a docid that is already committed, or a semantically redundant document supporting the same claim, unless it adds materially different evidence.

documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

reason.description: The distinct evidence, claim, perspective, date, name, counter-evidence, or coverage area this document uniquely contributes.

output.text:
Before COVID-19 upended daily life, only about 23 percent of US employees ever worked from home, and Pew Research found the figure closer to 7 percent for those doing so full time, meaning remote work was mostly a perk for highly paid white-collar professionals.

Global travel, in-person schooling, and face-to-face socializing were simply the unquestioned default, and video-conferencing tools existed but were used by a small niche rather than entire populations.

The origin story begins in Wuhan, China, where the first coronavirus cluster was reported on December 31, 2019, linked to the Huanan Seafood Market, and China became the first country to close schools nationwide on January 26, 2020.

By February 2020 the virus had been named COVID-19, cases had appeared in Thailand and the United States, and Italy and Iran emerged as major hotspots before the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a global pandemic on March 11, 2020.

Within days the United States declared a national emergency, and financial markets convulsed, with the Dow Jones posting three separate crashes in March 2020 known as "Black Monday I," "Black Thursday," and "Black Monday II," each wiping out roughly 8 to 13 percent of value in a single session.

Governments worldwide responded with sweeping lockdowns that shuttered businesses, closed borders, and confined populations to their homes, and the International Monetary Fund projected the global economy would shrink over 3 percent in 2020, the steepest slowdown since the Great Depression.

The World Bank later confirmed global GDP fell 5.2 percent in 2020, marking the first contraction of emerging-market economies since 1960 and pushing an estimated 70 to 100 million people into extreme poverty.

In the United States alone more than 36 million people filed for unemployment benefits within weeks, while European economies like France, Spain, and Italy saw GDP plunge by 17 to 21 percent in a single quarter.

Governments answered with historic stimulus, including the United States' $2 trillion CARES Act, worth roughly 10 percent of GDP, alongside comparable packages in Japan, Germany, and elsewhere.

Education was upended just as dramatically, with 1.7 billion students forced out of school worldwide, and studies in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Pakistan documented severe rural-urban learning gaps as remote instruction reached wealthier, better-connected households far more effectively than poorer ones.

A Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel report estimated a potential $17 trillion loss in lifetime earnings for the generation of affected schoolchildren, citing data showing Sao Paulo students in remote classes learned nearly 75 percent less than peers in person.

Air travel collapsed almost overnight, with global passenger traffic falling nearly 66 percent in 2020 according to IATA, industry net losses exceeding $118 billion, and carriers including Flybe, Virgin Australia, LATAM, and Avianca either ceasing operations or filing for bankruptcy.

Isolation and uncertainty triggered what researchers called a new mental health crisis, with depression rates nearly tripling to almost 30 percent in the pandemic's early months and drug overdose deaths topping 100,000 between April 2020 and April 2021.

Forced physical distancing reshaped social bonds as well, with academic analysis finding that people lost "weak ties" and gathered into smaller, more homogeneous networks, while everyday gestures like handshakes and hugs, as documented in Romania, were replaced by elbow bumps and distanced greetings.

Amid the devastation, technology adoption accelerated at unprecedented speed, as remote-work jumped almost overnight from about 7 percent to roughly a third of employed Americans, video-conferencing app downloads hit a record 62 million in a single week, and e-commerce, telemedicine, and e-learning platforms like Coursera all saw surging demand.

Hope arrived at the close of 2020 when Moderna and Pfizer/BioNTech announced highly effective vaccine candidates, with the FDA granting emergency authorization to Pfizer on December 11, 2020, Moderna a week later, and Johnson & Johnson in February 2021, delivering efficacy rates between 66 and 95 percent.

Throughout 2021 vaccine mandates spread rapidly across employers, healthcare systems, and the military, the United States hit President Biden's goal of 70 percent adult vaccination by early August, and boosters were rolled out for immunocompromised and elderly populations as the Delta and later Omicron variants eroded vaccine efficacy against infection.

A brief pause in Johnson & Johnson distribution in April 2021, prompted by rare blood-clot reports, was lifted within ten days after safety review, illustrating both the caution and resilience of the rollout.

As economies reopened, a global supply chain crisis and inflation surge followed, with commodity prices rising 31 to 60 percent above pre-pandemic levels, natural gas prices climbing over 500 percent, and a semiconductor shortage disrupting more than 169 industries according to Goldman Sachs research.

The labor market underwent its own upheaval as the "Great Resignation" saw more than 47 million Americans quit their jobs in 2021 alone, followed by "quiet quitting," a trend Gallup's 2022 workplace report linked to just 21 percent of employees feeling engaged and 44 percent reporting daily stress.

The United States formally ended its COVID-19 public health emergency declaration on May 11, 2023, symbolically marking the transition from pandemic crisis to an endemic, manageable disease.

By the mid-2020s, remote work had settled well below its pandemic peak but far above pre-2020 norms, with fully remote US workers falling to about 12 percent by 2023 even as roughly a quarter of the workforce retained some hybrid arrangement, and Upwork projecting 32.6 million Americans, about 22 percent of the workforce, would still work remotely by 2025.

This settling did not come without friction, as corporate leaders like Amazon's Andy Jassy pushed hard for full in-office returns, arguing employees perform better on-site despite acknowledging a lack of supporting data.

Education technology investment illustrated the scale of lasting change, projected to grow from $18 billion in 2019 to roughly $350 billion by 2025, even as most students returned to physical classrooms.

Long COVID emerged as a lasting medical legacy, with a large Scottish study finding persistent symptoms in 13.8 percent of infected people at six months and rising to 16.3 percent at eighteen months, while global estimates by 2024 placed the number of long-COVID sufferers above 65 million worldwide.

Even years later, COVID-19 continued to carry a higher mortality risk than seasonal influenza, underscoring that the disease's transition to endemic status did not mean it had become harmless.

Taken together, the arc from a near-total absence of remote work and digital healthcare in 2019 to a world where hybrid work, telehealth, e-learning, and lingering long-COVID burdens are permanent fixtures illustrates how thoroughly the pandemic reorganized public health systems, workplaces, schools, travel, economies, and social life within a single half-decade.

Global travel, in-person schooling, and face-to-face socializing were the unquestioned default, and video-conferencing tools existed but were used by a small niche rather than entire populations.
The origin story begins in Wuhan, China, where the first coronavirus cluster was reported on December 31, 2019, and China became the first country to close schools nationwide on January 26, 2020.
By February 2020 the virus had been named COVID-19 and cases had appeared in Thailand and the United States, and the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a global pandemic on March 11, 2020.

Within days the United States declared a national emergency, and financial markets convulsed, with the Dow Jones posting three separate crashes in March 2020 known as "Black Monday I," "Black Thursday," and "Black Monday II."

Governments worldwide responded with sweeping lockdowns, and the International Monetary Fund projected the global economy would shrink over 3 percent in 2020, the steepest slowdown since the Great Depression.

The World Bank later confirmed global GDP fell 5.2 percent in 2020, marking the first contraction of emerging-market economies since 1960 and pushing an estimated 70 to 100 million people into extreme poverty.

In the United States alone more than 36 million people filed for unemployment benefits within weeks, while European economies like France, Spain, and Italy saw GDP plunge by 17 to 21 percent in a single quarter.
Governments answered with historic stimulus, including the United States' $2 trillion CARES Act, worth roughly 10 percent of GDP, alongside comparable packages in Japan and Germany.

Education was upended just as dramatically, with 1.7 billion students forced out of school worldwide, and studies in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Pakistan documented severe rural-urban learning gaps as remote instruction reached wealthier households far more effectively than poorer ones.

A Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel report estimated a potential $17 trillion loss in lifetime earnings for affected schoolchildren, citing data showing Sao Paulo students in remote classes learned nearly 75 percent less than peers in person.

Air travel collapsed almost overnight, with global passenger traffic falling nearly 66 percent in 2020 according to IATA, industry net losses exceeding $118 billion, and carriers including Flybe, Virgin Australia, LATAM, and Avianca ceasing operations or filing for bankruptcy.

Isolation and uncertainty triggered a new mental health crisis, with depression rates nearly tripling to almost 30 percent in the pandemic's early months and drug overdose deaths topping 100,000 between April 2020 and April 2021.

Forced physical distancing reshaped social bonds, as academic analysis found people lost "weak ties" and gathered into smaller, more homogeneous networks, while everyday gestures like handshakes and hugs, documented in Romania, were replaced by elbow bumps and distanced greetings.

Amid the devastation, technology adoption accelerated at unprecedented speed, as remote work jumped almost overnight to roughly a third of employed Americans, video-conferencing app downloads hit a record 62 million in a single week, and e-commerce, telemedicine, and e-learning platforms all saw surging demand.

Hope arrived at the close of 2020 when Moderna and Pfizer/BioNTech announced highly effective vaccine candidates, with the FDA granting emergency authorization to Pfizer on December 11, 2020, Moderna a week later, and Johnson & Johnson in February 2021.

Throughout 2021 vaccine mandates spread across employers, healthcare systems, and the military, the United States hit President Biden's goal of 70 percent adult vaccination by early August, and boosters were rolled out as the Delta and later Omicron variants eroded vaccine efficacy against infection.

A brief pause in Johnson & Johnson distribution in April 2021, prompted by rare blood-clot reports, was lifted within ten days after safety review, illustrating both caution and resilience in the rollout.

As economies reopened, a global supply chain crisis and inflation surge followed, with commodity prices rising 31 to 60 percent above pre-pandemic levels, natural gas prices climbing over 500 percent, and a semiconductor shortage disrupting more than 169 industries.

The labor market underwent its own upheaval as the "Great Resignation" saw more than 47 million Americans quit their jobs in 2021 alone, followed by "quiet quitting," a trend Gallup's 2022 workplace report linked to just 21 percent of employees feeling engaged.
The United States formally ended its COVID-19 public health emergency declaration on May 11, 2023, marking the transition from pandemic crisis toward an endemic, manageable disease.

By the mid-2020s, remote work had settled well below its pandemic peak but far above pre-2020 norms, with fully remote US workers falling to about 12 percent by 2023 even as a quarter of the workforce retained hybrid arrangements, and Upwork projecting 32.6 million Americans would still work remotely by 2025.

This settling did not come without friction, as corporate leaders like Amazon's Andy Jassy pushed for full in-office returns, arguing employees perform better on-site despite acknowledging a lack of supporting data.

Education technology investment illustrated the scale of lasting change, projected to grow from $18 billion in 2019 to roughly $350 billion by 2025, even as most students returned to physical classrooms.

Long COVID emerged as a lasting medical legacy, with a large Scottish study finding persistent symptoms in 13.8 percent of infected people at six months, rising to 16.3 percent at eighteen months, while global estimates by 2024 placed long-COVID sufferers above 65 million worldwide.
Even years later, COVID-19 continued to carry a higher mortality risk than seasonal influenza, underscoring that its transition to endemic status did not mean the disease had become harmless.

Taken together, the arc from a near-total absence of remote work and digital healthcare in 2019 to a world where hybrid work, telehealth, e-learning, and lingering long-COVID burdens are permanent fixtures illustrates how thoroughly the pandemic reorganized public health, workplaces, schools, travel, economies, and social life within a single half-decade.
